title: From ER Diagram to Tables
html:
An Entity–Relationship model describes things and how they relate; a few mechanical rules turn it into tables, keys and foreign keys.

ER vocabulary

ER conceptBecomes
Entity (Customer, Product)A table
Attribute (name, price)A column
IdentifierPrimary key
Multivalued attribute (phone numbers)A separate child table
RelationshipA foreign key, or a junction table
Weak entity (Order line depends on Order)Table whose key includes the parent's key

Mapping relationships by cardinality

CardinalityExampleImplementation
One-to-one (1:1)Employee — Laptop allocation, User — ProfileFK with UNIQUE on one side (or share the same PK)
One-to-many (1:N)Department — Employees, Customer — OrdersFK on the many side (employees.dept_id)
Many-to-many (M:N)Orders — Products, Students — CoursesJunction table with two FKs (order_items)
RecursiveEmployee — ManagerFK to the same table (manager_id)

The sample database as an ER model

  • Department 1 : N Employee → employees.dept_id (nullable: Dev has none).
  • Employee 1 : N Employee (manages) → employees.manager_id.
  • Customer 1 : N Order → orders.customer_id (NOT NULL: every order has a customer).
  • Order M : N Product → junction table order_items (order_id, product_id) carrying relationship attributes quantity and unit_price.

Worked example: a course platform

Watch out

Never model many-to-many with a comma-separated list or with course1, course2, course3 columns — you can't index, join, constrain or count them properly. Always use a junction table.

How do you implement a many-to-many relationship?

With a junction (bridge/associative) table holding a foreign key to each side, whose primary key is usually the pair of FKs (PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)). Attributes of the relationship itself (grade, quantity, enrolled date) live in the junction table.
